1.why: Speed is distance divided by time (v = s ÷ t).

wrong.b: Multiplying distance by time is wrong.
wrong.d: Dividing time by distance is upside down.

2.why: Strong wind speed determines how fast weather systems and hazards travel.

wrong.a: Low temperature does not define speed.

3.why: Meteorological agencies track storm tracks and wind speeds to issue timely warnings.

wrong.b: Solar panels do not track storms.
wrong.d: Tides are separate from wind speed.

_quiz_pool.question: What does v stand for in v = s ÷ t?
_quiz_pool.explanation: v represents speed, measured in metres per second (m/s).

_quiz_pool.question: If a weather front travels 1,200 metres in 40 seconds, what is its speed?
_quiz_pool.explanation: 1,200 m divided by 40 s equals 30 m/s.

_quiz_pool.question: What is the SI unit of distance s?
Which agency coordinates worldwide weather observations?
_quiz_pool.explanation: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) coordinates global weather monitoring.

_quiz_pool.question: What does t represent in the speed formula?
_quiz_pool.explanation: t stands for time elapsed, measured in seconds (s).

_quiz_pool.question: Why do weather agencies monitor storm wind speeds?
_quiz_pool.explanation: Tracking speed helps protect lives and property through early warnings.

must_show: a light paper streamer or ribbon outdoors
a stopwatch measuring how long it takes to flutter across a measured distance
student hands holding the tools safely

story.title: Tracking fast-moving storms
story.lead: Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a particular time, defined by temperature, precipitation, pressure, wind and humidity [1]. Extreme weather events can have serious impacts on society [1].
story.image_caption: Coastal weather monitoring from Earth observation satellites

story.body_1: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) coordinates global observations to produce timely weather forecasts and early warning systems [1]. Weather describes short-term events that require forecasts to plan daily life and prepare for hazards [1].
story.body_2: Natural hazard research provides global data that enhance our assessment and predictive capabilities to anticipate and reduce risks [2]. Coastal and marine ecosystems also face pressure from climate change and storms [3].

physics.title: Measuring weather speed
physics.body_1: To understand how fast a weather system or wind front moves, scientists measure the distance it travels and how long it takes.
physics.body_2: Speed tells us how many metres something moves in each second. Knowing this helps predict when a storm will strike.
physics.assumptions: We assume the weather front travels at a steady speed over the measured straight-line distance.

lab.label: MINI LAB · TRY AT HOME OR SCHOOL
lab.title: Measure wind speed with a streamer
lab.subtitle: Use a light paper ribbon and a stopwatch to test how wind speed moves objects outdoors.
lab.step_1: Measure a 10-metre track outdoors where there is a gentle breeze.
lab.st1_sub: Mark the start and finish lines clearly.
lab.step_2: Hold a light paper streamer and time how long it takes the breeze to carry your marker across.
lab.st2_sub: Record the time t in seconds.
lab.step_3: Calculate speed v = s ÷ t to find the wind speed.
lab.st3_sub: Compare results on calm and breezy days.
